content: Sickle cell disease is a recessively inherited disorder of hemoglobin that predominantly affects individuals from regions such as sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, the Mediterranean basin, the Indian subcontinent, the Caribbean, and South America. This condition is associated with significant complications and a reduced life expectancy. Phytomedicines, which are plant-derived medicines used in their natural state, include many traditional remedies that are commonly encountered by populations most affected by this disease. Laboratory studies and limited clinical trials have indicated potential positive effects of phytomedicines in both in vivo and in vitro settings. However, there has been minimal systematic evaluation of their benefits. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and risks of phytomedicines in individuals with sickle cell disease, regardless of age, type of disease, or setting. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, the International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number Register (ISRCTN), the Allied and Complementary Medicine Database (AMED), ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The most recent searches were conducted between March 2020 and July 2020, depending on the database. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized trials involving participants of all ages with sickle cell disease. These trials compared the administration of phytomedicines, delivered through any mode, to either placebo or conventional treatments such as blood transfusion or hydroxyurea. The quality of the trials was independently assessed by two authors, and data were extracted accordingly. Three trials involving a total of 212 participants were included in the review. These trials evaluated three different phytomedicines: Niprisan® (also known as Nicosan®), Ciklavit®, and a powdered extract of Pfaffia paniculata. 1. Niprisan®: A Phase IIB (pivotal) trial suggested that Niprisan® may be effective in reducing episodes of severe painful sickle cell disease crises over a six-month period. However, the evidence supporting this finding was of low quality. Niprisan® did not appear to influence the risk of severe complications or the degree of anemia, based on low-quality evidence. No adverse effects were reported with its use. 2. Ciklavit®: A single trial of Cajanus cajan (Ciklavit®) indicated a potential benefit in reducing painful crises. However, there was a possible, though statistically non-significant, adverse effect on anemia levels. The evidence supporting these findings was of low quality. 3. Pfaffia paniculata: The effects of Pfaffia paniculata on laboratory parameters and symptoms of sickle cell disease remain uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. No adverse effects were reported with its use. The authors concluded that Niprisan® appeared to be safe and potentially effective in reducing severe painful crises over a six-month follow-up period. However, further trials are necessary to confirm its role in managing sickle cell disease, and the results of ongoing multicenter trials are awaited. Currently, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the efficacy of Ciklavit® or the powdered root extract of Pfaffia paniculata in managing sickle cell disease. Overall, while phytomedicines may have a potential beneficial effect in reducing painful crises in sickle cell disease, this needs to be validated through additional trials with improved study designs and more robust data collection. Further research is required to establish the safety and efficacy of these plant-based treatments in managing this condition.
